headline: HC freezes S Alam Group’s 81.92% shares in Islami Bank
summary: The High Court ordered a three-month freeze on the shares after allegations that the group illegally consolidated control of the bank.
details: The High Court has ordered the authorities to freeze 81.92 percent of S Alam Group's shares in Islami Bank Bangladesh for three months.
The order comes amid allegations that the shares were illegally consolidated and controlled by the group through 24 different companies.
A writ petition was filed by the Islamic Economic Research Bureau (IERB), a sponsor shareholder of the bank, leading to the High Court's decision.
Under the Bank Company Act of 1991, a single group or family is prohibited from holding more than 10 percent of a bank's shares.
The petition alleges that 24 companies linked to S Alam Group held a combined stake of 81.92 percent, far exceeding the legal limit.
The court has questioned why the Bangladesh Bank's inaction in preventing this concentration of shares should not be declared illegal.
The High Court has also questioned why the shares held in excess of the permissible limit should not be forfeited under the law.
caption:
81.92% of Islami Bank shares held by S Alam Group are now frozen by the High Court.

The High Court has ordered the authorities to freeze 81.92 percent of S Alam Group's shares in Islami Bank Bangladesh for three months.

The order comes amid allegations that the shares were illegally consolidated and controlled by the group through 24 different companies.

A writ petition was filed by the Islamic Economic Research Bureau (IERB), a sponsor shareholder of the bank, leading to the High Court's decision.

Under the Bank Company Act of 1991, a single group or family is prohibited from holding more than 10 percent of a bank's shares.

The petition alleges that 24 companies linked to S Alam Group held a combined stake of 81.92 percent, far exceeding the legal limit.

The court has questioned why the Bangladesh Bank's inaction in preventing this concentration of shares should not be declared illegal.

The High Court has also questioned why the shares held in excess of the permissible limit should not be forfeited under the law.

headline_marked: Uber [[lays off 3,300 corporate employees]] in largest cut since pandemic
headline: Uber lays off 3,300 corporate employees in largest cut since pandemic
summary: The US-based ride-sharing giant is cutting 10% of its global corporate workforce to streamline management and invest in autonomous technology.
details: Ride-sharing giant Uber has announced the layoff of approximately 3,300 corporate employees, representing 10% of its global corporate workforce. This marks the company's largest workforce reduction since the 2020 pandemic.

CEO Dara Khosrowshahi informed staff in a letter, stating the move is intended to make Uber a simpler and more agile organization. The company aims to reduce administrative complexity and decrease the number of micro-teams by nearly 50%.

Alongside the layoffs, Uber is implementing a strict return-to-office policy. Approximately 99% of employees must now work from the office at least three days a week, with remote work opportunities limited to less than 1% of staff.

The company is shifting its investment focus toward future technology. Uber plans to spend $10 billion on 'Robotaxis' (autonomous vehicles) and has already partnered with the UK-based autonomous vehicle maker Wayve.
To strengthen its position in the food delivery market, Uber Eats has agreed to acquire the German company Delivery Hero for $14.8 billion to better compete with rivals like DoorDash.
Founded in San Francisco in 2010, Uber currently has a market value exceeding $150 billion. Its last major layoff occurred in 2020, when 6,700 employees lost their jobs due to the pandemic.
